questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient identification)
questions.q: Before recording a 12-lead EKG, how does the technician confirm the patient's identity?
options: Two identifiers checked against the order
The room number on the door
The name on the bed's whiteboard
Asking "Are you Mr. Jones?" and waiting for a yes
questions.explain: Two patient-specific identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, are matched with the order and ID band. Room numbers and yes-or-no questions do not reliably identify a patient.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient identification)
questions.q: The name on the EKG order does not match the patient's ID band. What should the technician do?
options: Record it and fix the name later
Use the name on the ID band only
Ask the patient which name is right
questions.explain: A mismatch between the order and the ID band must be resolved with the nurse or ordering provider before testing, so the tracing is not filed under the wrong patient.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (explaining the procedure)
questions.q: A patient asks whether the EKG machine will send electricity into his body. What is the best response?
options: Yes, but the current is very small and safe
Only if the heart rhythm is abnormal
No, it only records the heart's own signals
Yes, which is why it may tingle
questions.explain: An EKG is a passive recording of the electrical activity the heart produces. No current is delivered to the patient, which is a common worry worth addressing before the test.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (explaining the procedure)
questions.q: Why does the technician explain the EKG procedure before starting?
options: To meet the department time limit for the whole test
To ask the patient to interpret it
To ease anxiety and get the patient's cooperation
questions.explain: Explaining what will happen reduces anxiety and muscle tension, which also reduces artifact, and gives the patient a chance to ask questions or decline.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (privacy)
questions.q: How can the technician protect a patient's privacy during electrode placement?
options: Leave the door open for others to see
Close the curtain and expose only what is needed
Remove the gown completely for the entire recording time
Ask visitors to stay and hold the gown
questions.explain: Closing the door or curtain and draping so that only the needed areas are exposed protects dignity. Visitors may stay only if the patient wishes.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (privacy)
questions.q: When placing chest electrodes on a female patient, how can modesty be preserved?
options: Ask her to remove all upper clothing for the test
Keep her draped and uncover only as needed
Place the chest leads over the gown
Skip V4 through V6 if she is shy
questions.explain: The patient stays draped and only the needed area is uncovered briefly; electrodes are placed on the skin, not over clothing. Leads cannot be skipped to save time or embarrassment.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (infection control)
questions.q: When should the technician perform hand hygiene during an EKG?
options: Only after removing the electrodes at the end
Before and after contact with each patient
Only if the patient looks ill
Only at the start of each shift
questions.explain: Hand hygiene is performed before and after patient contact and after removing gloves, as part of standard precautions. Infection is not always visible, so appearance does not matter.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (infection control)
questions.q: How should EKG lead wires and cables be handled between patients?
options: Clean them with an approved disinfectant
Wipe them with a dry paper towel from the sink
Rinse them under running tap water
Clean them once a month only
questions.explain: Reusable lead wires contact patients' skin and can carry organisms, so they are cleaned with a facility-approved disinfectant between patients, following the manufacturer's guidance.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (infection control)
questions.q: What is done with disposable EKG electrodes after the test?
options: Store them for the next patient
Return them to the open package
questions.explain: Disposable electrodes are single use. Reusing them risks infection and poor contact from used gel, which can also cause artifact.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (transmission-based precautions)
questions.q: An EKG is ordered for a patient on contact precautions. What should the technician do?
options: Wear no PPE because the test is brief and noninvasive
Wear gown and gloves and disinfect equipment after
Wear a mask only and skip disinfection
Ask the patient to come to the hallway
questions.explain: Contact precautions require a gown and gloves on entry. The machine and cables are disinfected after use, or dedicated equipment is used, to avoid spreading organisms to other patients.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient distress)
questions.q: During a resting EKG, the patient reports new chest pain. What should the technician do?
options: Stay with the patient and alert the nurse or provider
Finish the full test first and mention the pain at the end
Tell the patient to stay still and stop talking
Leave the room to look for a chair
questions.explain: New chest pain may signal a cardiac emergency. The technician stays with the patient, gets help immediately, and may be asked to record or repeat a tracing during the pain.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient distress)
questions.q: A patient becomes unresponsive during an EKG and has no pulse. What should the technician do?
options: Go to find the ordering provider
Call a code and begin CPR
questions.explain: An unresponsive patient without a pulse is in cardiac arrest. The technician activates the emergency response and starts CPR right away, using an AED as soon as one arrives.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (reporting critical findings)
questions.q: The technician sees a rhythm that looks like ventricular tachycardia on a responsive patient's tracing. What is the correct action?
options: Print it and place it in the provider inbox for later
Notify the licensed provider or nurse at once
Tell the patient the rhythm is dangerous
questions.explain: Potentially life-threatening rhythms are reported immediately to the licensed provider or nurse, following facility protocol, while the technician stays with the patient. Technicians do not interpret results for patients.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (reporting critical findings)
questions.q: After notifying the nurse about an abnormal tracing, what should the technician document?
options: Who was notified, when and what was reported
Only that the tracing looked bad
Nothing, since the nurse was told
The technician's diagnosis of the rhythm
questions.explain: Documentation of critical communication includes the name of the person notified, the time and the information given. This creates a record that the finding was acted on.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (scope of practice)
questions.q: After the EKG, the patient asks, "Is my heart OK?" What is the best response?
options: The provider will review it and talk with you
Your heart looks perfectly normal to me
You definitely had a heart attack before
I am not allowed to tell you anything about it ever
questions.explain: Interpreting results and giving a diagnosis are the provider's role. The technician explains that the provider will review the tracing and discuss it, without being dismissive.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (equipment safety)
questions.q: The technician notices the EKG machine's power cord is frayed. What should be done?
options: Wrap the cord in tape and keep using it
Take it out of service and report it
Use it only for short tracings today
Unplug it while recording to be safe
questions.explain: Damaged cords create shock and fire hazards. The equipment is tagged out of service and reported according to facility policy for biomedical repair.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (equipment safety)
questions.q: Which practice supports electrical safety when using an EKG machine plugged into the wall?
options: Remove the ground prong if it does not fit
Use a properly grounded three-prong outlet
Plug in with wet hands to save time
questions.explain: Properly grounded hospital-grade outlets reduce shock risk and electrical interference. Extension cords, missing ground prongs and wet hands all increase hazards.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (HIPAA)
questions.q: A completed EKG tracing is left on a counter in a public hallway. What is the problem?
options: It may fade under the hallway lights
It is too early to give to the provider
It may be filed in the wrong order
questions.explain: EKG tracings carry patient identifiers and health information, so they must be kept secure and delivered only to authorized staff. Leaving them in public areas is a privacy violation.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (HIPAA)
questions.q: A visitor in the hallway asks the technician what a patient's EKG showed. What should the technician do?
options: Share the result if the visitor is family
Share the rhythm name but not the details
Show the tracing quickly without comment
Decline and refer questions to the care team
questions.explain: Health information is shared only with people the patient has authorized, through the appropriate care team. The technician does not discuss results with visitors.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (HIPAA)
questions.q: Which practice protects electronic EKG records?
options: Sharing a password among the night shift
Logging out of the EKG cart after each use
Saving tracings to a personal flash drive
Taking phone photos of tracings for review
questions.explain: Unique logins, logging out and storing tracings only in approved systems protect electronic health information. Shared passwords and personal devices break security rules.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (documentation)
questions.q: Which information should appear on every EKG tracing?
options: Only the date the test was performed
Only the room number and bed letter
Patient name, identifier, date and time
questions.explain: Each tracing must be clearly identified with the patient's name and identifier and the date and time, so it can be compared with earlier tracings and filed correctly.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (coordinated patient care)
questions.q: For a patient with suspected acute coronary syndrome arriving at the emergency department, within about how long is a 12-lead EKG commonly expected?
questions.explain: Guidelines call for a 12-lead EKG within about 10 minutes of arrival for patients with symptoms suggesting acute coronary syndrome, so treatment for a heart attack is not delayed.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (coordinated patient care)
questions.q: A stat EKG is ordered. What does stat mean?
questions.explain: Stat means immediately. Stat EKGs are prioritized over routine orders because they are usually ordered for urgent problems such as chest pain.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (coordinated patient care)
questions.q: A patient has a pacemaker. Why should this be noted with the EKG?
options: The test must be canceled for the patient's safety
Only lead aVR can be recorded
The device changes how the tracing looks
questions.explain: Paced beats show pacemaker spikes and often wide QRS complexes, so noting the device helps the reader interpret the tracing correctly. A pacemaker is not a reason to cancel an EKG.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (coordinated patient care)
questions.q: Why is it helpful to note certain cardiac medications, such as digoxin, when an EKG is recorded?
options: Some drugs can change the tracing
The machine needs the dose to print
Patients on them cannot have an EKG
questions.explain: Several drugs affect heart rate, intervals and ST segments, so noting them per facility policy helps the provider interpret the tracing. They do not prevent the test.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient safety)
questions.q: An older patient is unsteady getting onto the exam table for an EKG. What should the technician do?
options: Let the patient climb up alone
Record the EKG with the patient standing
Help the patient and use a step stool
Ask a visitor to lift the patient
questions.explain: Fall prevention includes assisting unsteady patients, using a stable step and locking the table or bed. If the patient cannot get onto the table, the EKG can be recorded in a chair or bed.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient safety)
questions.q: A patient arrives in a wheelchair for an EKG. What is done before helping the patient transfer?
questions.explain: Locking the brakes keeps the wheelchair from rolling during the transfer, preventing falls. The table or bed is also kept locked and at a safe height.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient safety)
questions.q: A patient reports a latex allergy before an EKG. What should the technician do?
options: Proceed because EKGs never use latex
Ask the patient to wear long sleeves
Reschedule the test for another day
questions.explain: Some gloves, tourniquets and supplies contain latex. The technician uses latex-free products and follows facility allergy procedures; the EKG itself can proceed.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient distress)
questions.q: During setup, a patient becomes pale, sweaty and dizzy while sitting up. What should the technician do first?
options: Ask the patient to stand up and walk it off slowly
Give the patient a cup of hot coffee
Leave to find a blood pressure cuff
Help the patient lie down and call for help
questions.explain: Lying the patient down protects against a fall from fainting, and summoning help gets a clinician to assess the cause. The technician stays with the patient.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (communication)
questions.q: A patient is deaf and reads lips. How should the technician explain the EKG?
options: Face the patient and speak clearly
Explain only to the patient's visitor
questions.explain: Facing the patient in good light and speaking clearly at a normal pace helps lip reading; written notes or an interpreter can also be used. Shouting distorts lip movements.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (communication)
questions.q: A patient speaks only Spanish and the technician does not. What is the best way to explain the EKG?
questions.explain: A qualified interpreter, in person, by phone or video, lets the patient understand and agree to the test. Other patients cannot be used as interpreters because of privacy and accuracy concerns.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (communication)
questions.q: A young child is frightened before an EKG. Which approach is best?
options: Hold the child down without explaining
Tell the child the test will hurt a lot
Send the parent out of the room first
Explain simply and let a parent stay close
questions.explain: Simple honest explanations, letting the child see or touch an electrode and keeping a parent nearby reduce fear and movement artifact.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient distress)
questions.q: A patient is very anxious and the heart rate is fast on the monitor before the EKG. What can the technician do?
options: Reassure and help the patient relax
Tell the patient to hold the breath
Ask the patient to tense the arms
questions.explain: Explaining the test, keeping the patient warm and covered and encouraging slow, normal breathing helps the patient relax, which also reduces muscle artifact.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (consent)
questions.q: A patient refuses an ordered EKG after it is explained. What should the technician do?
options: Perform the EKG anyway because the provider ordered it
Ask a family member to sign for the patient
Hold the patient's arms to place the leads
Respect the refusal and notify the nurse or provider
questions.explain: Competent patients may refuse procedures. The technician does not proceed, informs the nurse or provider so they can discuss it, and documents the refusal per policy.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (consent)
questions.q: How does a patient usually give consent for a routine EKG?
options: A separate written surgical consent form signed by a witness
Implied consent by cooperating after an explanation
A court order from a judge
questions.explain: For routine, noninvasive procedures, consent is usually implied when the patient cooperates after the procedure is explained. The patient can withdraw that consent at any time.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (telemetry)
questions.q: A telemetry monitor alarms for a dangerous rhythm. What should be checked first?
questions.explain: Alarms are first answered by looking at the patient, because the rhythm may be real. Only after the patient is assessed are leads, batteries and connections checked for artifact.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (telemetry)
questions.q: Why should telemetry alarms never be turned off or silenced without following policy?
options: Alarms help the monitor save battery
The alarm sound calibrates the leads
A real emergency could be missed
questions.explain: Disabled or ignored alarms can lead to missed life-threatening rhythms. Alarm limits are set and changed only according to facility policy and orders.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (stress testing)
questions.q: Why must emergency equipment be readily available during an exercise stress test?
options: The treadmill often loses power during testing
Exercise can trigger ischemia or arrhythmias
questions.explain: Stress testing deliberately increases cardiac workload, which can provoke chest pain, ischemia or dangerous rhythms. A defibrillator, emergency medications and trained staff are kept ready.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (stress testing)
questions.q: During a treadmill stress test, the patient reports severe chest pain and dizziness. What should the technician do?
options: Encourage the patient to keep walking
Increase the speed to finish sooner
Note it and review it after the test
questions.explain: Severe chest pain or dizziness are warning signs, and the supervising provider decides on stopping the test, which is usually done. The technician reports symptoms immediately and keeps monitoring.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (infection control)
questions.q: A disposable razor was used to remove chest hair before electrode placement. How is it discarded?
questions.explain: Razors are sharps and go into a puncture-resistant sharps container. Many facilities prefer clippers, which lower the risk of nicks.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (compliance)
questions.q: The technician is unsure whether an order is for a 12-lead EKG or a rhythm strip. What should be done?
options: Record whichever test is faster to finish on the unit
Clarify the order with the nurse or provider
Record both and bill for both
Ask the patient which one to do
questions.explain: When an order is unclear, the technician clarifies it before performing the test. Guessing may lead to the wrong test and delayed care.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (compliance)
questions.q: A technician wants to share an interesting EKG tracing on social media with the name removed. What is the concern?
options: EKGs are public records that anyone may post online
It is fine if the hospital is named
Other details may still identify the patient
It is fine if posted after hours only
questions.explain: Even without a name, dates, locations or unusual details may identify a patient, and posting patient information without authorization violates policy and privacy law.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (abuse and neglect)
questions.q: During electrode placement, the technician notices bruises in different stages of healing on an older patient. What should the technician do?
options: Ignore it because it is not related to the heart
Ask the family member to explain it
Report the observation per facility policy
Post a note on the patient's door
questions.explain: Unexplained injuries can indicate abuse or neglect. The technician reports objective observations to the nurse or supervisor according to facility policy, which addresses mandated reporting.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (infection control)
questions.q: The technician must enter the room of a patient on airborne precautions for an EKG. Which protection is required?
questions.explain: Airborne precautions, used for diseases such as tuberculosis or measles, require a fit-tested N95 or higher respirator before entering. A surgical mask does not filter small airborne particles adequately.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (patient identification)
questions.q: An outpatient arrives for an EKG. How should identity be confirmed?
options: Ask the patient to state name and birth date
Say the patient's name and wait for a nod
Check the name on the parking ticket
Ask which doctor ordered the test
questions.explain: Open-ended questions asking the patient to state their full name and date of birth avoid errors from patients agreeing to the wrong name. The answers are compared with the order.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (equipment safety)
questions.q: Why is EKG equipment routinely inspected by biomedical engineering?
options: To change the paper roll each week
To confirm it is safe and works correctly
To clean the lead wires between patients
questions.explain: Scheduled preventive maintenance and electrical safety checks confirm that the machine records accurately and does not leak current. Cleaning and paper changes are the user's routine tasks.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (coordinated patient care)
questions.q: The provider asks for a comparison with a prior EKG. Why is it important that tracings are correctly labeled and filed?
options: Old tracings are used to set the paper speed
Changes over time help with diagnosis
Filing order sets the heart rate
It allows tracings to be reused
questions.explain: Comparing a new tracing with earlier ones shows whether findings are new or old, which affects decisions. Mislabeled tracings could lead to wrong conclusions.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), Safety, Compliance and Coordinated Patient Care (body mechanics)
questions.q: How should the technician adjust the bed before placing electrodes on a patient in bed?
options: Lower it all the way down to the floor level
Raise it to a comfortable working height
questions.explain: Raising the bed to waist height reduces back strain for the technician. The bed is lowered again and the call light left in reach when finished.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: How many electrodes are placed on the patient to record a standard 12-lead EKG?
questions.explain: A standard 12-lead EKG uses 10 electrodes: four on the limbs and six on the chest. The machine combines them to produce 12 different views, or leads, of the heart.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V1 electrode placed?
options: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
Second intercostal space, right sternal border
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
questions.explain: V1 goes in the fourth intercostal space just to the right of the sternum. V2 mirrors it on the left side, and V4 sits in the fifth space at the midclavicular line.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V2 electrode placed?
options: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, left anterior axillary line
Third intercostal space, left midclavicular line
questions.explain: V2 is in the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border, directly across from V1. Placing V1 and V2 too high is a common error that changes the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V4 electrode placed?
questions.explain: V4 sits in the fifth intercostal space on the left midclavicular line. V5 and V6 are placed at the same horizontal level as V4 at the anterior and midaxillary lines.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V3 electrode placed?
questions.explain: V3 is placed halfway between V2 and V4, so V4 is usually located first. V5 lies between V4 and V6.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V5 electrode placed?
options: Left anterior axillary line, level with V4
Left midaxillary line, level with V4
Right anterior axillary line, level with V4
questions.explain: V5 goes on the left anterior axillary line at the same horizontal level as V4. V6 is on the midaxillary line at that level.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Where is the V6 electrode placed?
options: Left midaxillary line, level with V4
Left anterior axillary line, level with V4
Left posterior axillary line, sixth space
Right midaxillary line, level with V4
questions.explain: V6 sits on the left midaxillary line, level with V4 and V5. Placing it too low or too far back is a common error.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Which landmark helps the technician locate the second intercostal space when counting down to V1?
questions.explain: The sternal angle, or angle of Louis, is the ridge where the manubrium meets the sternal body; the second rib attaches there, and the space below it is the second intercostal space. Counting down from there finds the fourth space.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: What is the midclavicular line?
options: A horizontal line drawn across the chest at the nipples
A line down the center of the sternum
A line from the armpit to the hip
A vertical line through the middle of the clavicle
questions.explain: The midclavicular line runs straight down from the midpoint of the clavicle and is used to place V4. The midsternal line runs down the center of the sternum.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (limb leads)
questions.q: Which limb electrode serves as the ground or reference electrode?
questions.explain: The right leg electrode acts as a ground or reference and does not form part of any limb lead. Leads I, II and III are formed from the right arm, left arm and left leg.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (limb leads)
questions.q: For a resting EKG, where are limb electrodes generally placed?
options: On fleshy areas of the arms and legs
On the chest near the collarbones
On the palms and the soles
questions.explain: Limb electrodes are placed on fleshy, flat areas of the limbs, avoiding bone, to get good contact and less artifact. Placement should be symmetrical on both sides.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (limb leads)
questions.q: A patient has a left leg amputation below the knee. Where is the left leg electrode placed?
options: On the right leg, next to the right leg electrode
On the left arm below the left arm lead
It is left off and the EKG is recorded
On the residual limb, with the right matching it
questions.explain: The electrode is placed on the residual limb, and the opposite electrode is placed at a matching level to keep the leads balanced. The modification is noted on the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: Which leads are the standard bipolar limb leads?
questions.explain: Leads I, II and III each compare a positive and negative limb electrode, so they are bipolar. The augmented leads aVR, aVL and aVF and the precordial leads are unipolar.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: How are leads aVR, aVL and aVF classified?
questions.explain: The augmented leads compare one limb electrode with a combination of the others, and the machine amplifies the signal. They are limb leads, not chest leads.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: Which leads are the precordial leads?
questions.explain: The precordial, or chest, leads are V1 through V6, placed across the chest to view the heart in the horizontal plane. The limb leads view it in the frontal plane.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: Which electrodes form lead I?
questions.explain: Lead I records between the right arm (negative) and the left arm (positive). Lead II uses right arm and left leg, and lead III uses left arm and left leg.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: Which lead is most often used for a continuous rhythm strip?
questions.explain: Lead II usually shows clear, upright P waves and QRS complexes, so it is commonly used for rhythm strips and monitoring. Other leads may be used when ordered.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead types)
questions.q: Which triangle describes the relationship of leads I, II and III?
questions.explain: Einthoven's triangle is formed by the right arm, left arm and left leg, with leads I, II and III as its sides. The femoral triangle and the triangle of Koch are anatomic regions.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (calibration)
questions.q: At standard calibration, how tall is the calibration mark for 1 millivolt?
questions.explain: Standard calibration makes 1 mV produce a 10 mm deflection, or two large boxes. Half standard produces 5 mm and double standard produces 20 mm.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (calibration)
questions.q: QRS complexes are so tall that they overlap the leads above and below. Which adjustment is commonly made?
options: Change to double standard and note it
Turn off all filters on the machine
Change to half standard and note it
questions.explain: Half standard, 5 mm per mV, shrinks very tall complexes so they fit. The change must be noted on the tracing so the reader measures voltage correctly.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (calibration)
questions.q: What does the standard calibration pulse look like at the start of a tracing?
questions.explain: At standard settings the calibration pulse is a rectangle, or square wave, 10 mm tall. Its shape and height confirm that the machine is calibrated correctly.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (paper speed)
questions.q: What is the standard paper speed for a 12-lead EKG?
questions.explain: The standard speed is 25 mm per second, which makes each small box equal 0.04 seconds. Changing the speed changes the time each box represents.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (paper speed)
questions.q: A tracing is accidentally recorded at 50 mm/s. How do the complexes appear?
options: Wider, with intervals that look longer
Narrower, with intervals that look shorter
questions.explain: At 50 mm/s the paper moves twice as fast, spreading each complex across twice as many boxes, so intervals look twice as long. Voltage is not affected.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (EKG paper)
questions.q: What type of paper does a standard EKG machine use?
questions.explain: EKG machines commonly print with a heated stylus or thermal printhead on heat-sensitive grid paper. The grid lets the reader measure time and voltage.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: A tracing shows a thick, regular, fuzzy baseline in several leads. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: AC interference produces a regular, fine, thick baseline from nearby electrical equipment, poor grounding or crossed cables. Breathing causes a wandering baseline instead.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: Which action helps reduce alternating current interference?
options: Have the patient hold the metal bed rails firmly
Coil the lead wires tightly together
Move the machine onto the patient
questions.explain: Moving away from or unplugging nearby electrical devices, checking grounding and keeping lead wires untangled reduce AC interference. Touching metal bed rails can make it worse.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: A shivering patient's tracing shows irregular, jagged spikes. What is this artifact?
questions.explain: Somatic tremor, or muscle artifact, comes from muscle activity such as shivering, tension, talking or tremors. Warming and relaxing the patient usually reduces it.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: A patient with a hand tremor shows muscle artifact in the limb leads. What can help?
options: Move chest electrodes toward the abdomen
Move limb electrodes closer to the trunk
Have the patient grip the bed rails
questions.explain: Placing limb electrodes on the upper arms and thighs, away from the trembling hands, often reduces tremor artifact. The placement is noted on the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: The baseline slowly drifts up and down with each breath. What is this artifact called?
questions.explain: A wandering baseline moves up and down, often with breathing, poor electrode contact or lotion on the skin. Good skin prep and asking the patient to breathe normally help.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: One lead shows a flat line while the others look normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: The paper speed is too high
The calibration is set to half
questions.explain: A flat line in only one lead points to a loose electrode or broken wire, called an interrupted baseline. True asystole would appear in every lead and the patient would be unresponsive.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: In lead I, the P wave and QRS are both inverted on an adult with a normal heart position. What is a likely technical cause?
options: Paper speed is set to 50 mm/s instead of 25
Calibration is set to half standard
Right and left arm electrodes are reversed
Chest leads V5 and V6 are swapped
questions.explain: Reversing the arm electrodes flips lead I, inverting the P wave and QRS. Before removing electrodes, the technician checks the tracing and corrects any reversal.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (skin preparation)
questions.q: Why is the skin cleaned and lightly abraded before electrode placement?
options: To remove oil and dead skin for good contact
To numb the skin before the electrodes are applied
To mark the electrode sites in ink
To warm the skin for the patient
questions.explain: Oils, lotion and dead skin cells increase resistance and cause artifact. Cleaning and gentle abrasion improve electrode contact and signal quality.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (skin preparation)
questions.q: A patient has heavy chest hair at the V3 and V4 sites. What should the technician do?
options: Place the electrodes over the hair
Move those leads to the abdomen
Use extra tape over the electrodes
Clip or shave a small area per policy
questions.explain: Hair prevents good contact, so a small area is clipped or shaved per facility policy. Moving electrodes away from the correct sites changes the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (skin preparation)
questions.q: A patient is very sweaty and electrodes keep falling off. What helps?
options: Apply lotion to the skin to help them stick better
Add water to the electrode gel
Place them on top of the gown
Dry the skin well before placing them
questions.explain: Electrodes adhere poorly to moist skin, so the skin is dried thoroughly; some facilities allow additional prep steps. Lotion and water make adhesion worse.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (supplies)
questions.q: Why should the technician check that electrodes are not dried out before use?
options: Dry electrodes give the patient a shock
Dry gel gives poor contact and artifact
Dry gel changes the paper speed
Dry electrodes make the leads reverse
questions.explain: Electrodes with dried gel conduct poorly and cause artifact. Packages are kept sealed and used before the expiration date, since gel dries out once a package is opened or ages.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (patient positioning)
questions.q: How is a patient usually positioned for a resting 12-lead EKG?
options: Supine with arms relaxed at the sides
Prone with arms under the chest
questions.explain: The patient lies supine and relaxed, arms at the sides and legs uncrossed, to reduce muscle artifact. If the patient cannot lie flat, the position is adjusted and noted.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (patient positioning)
questions.q: A patient with breathing difficulty cannot lie flat for an EKG. What should be done?
options: Insist that the patient lie flat
Record it with the patient standing
Raise the head of the bed and note it
questions.explain: The EKG can be recorded in a semi-Fowler or sitting position for comfort. The position is noted because it can slightly affect the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (patient instructions)
questions.q: Which instruction helps reduce artifact during recording?
options: Lie still, breathe normally and do not talk
Hold your breath until the recording is finished
Tighten your arm muscles during it
Keep your legs crossed during it
questions.explain: Lying still, breathing normally and not talking keeps muscle activity low. Holding the breath and tensing muscles can cause artifact.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: How are chest electrodes placed on a patient with large breasts?
options: On the chest wall beneath the breast tissue
On top of the breast at the nipple level
Higher on the chest above the breasts
On the abdomen below the ribs
questions.explain: Common guidance is to place V4 through V6 on the chest wall under the breast, at their correct landmarks, rather than on breast tissue. Moving electrodes up or down changes the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (special situations)
questions.q: A provider orders a right-sided EKG. Where is lead V4R placed?
options: Right fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
Left fifth intercostal space, midaxillary line
Right second intercostal space, sternal border
Left fourth intercostal space, sternal border
questions.explain: Right-sided leads mirror the standard left chest placements, so V4R goes in the right fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The tracing is labeled as right-sided.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (special situations)
questions.q: Which change is commonly made when recording an EKG on an infant?
options: Use adult electrodes placed on the abdomen instead
Place all leads on one arm
Use smaller electrodes suited to the chest
questions.explain: Small pediatric electrodes fit the small chest and avoid overlapping. Placement follows the same landmarks, and the patient's age is entered into the machine.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (special situations)
questions.q: Electrodes cannot be placed on a site because of a bandage over a wound on the left arm. What is done?
options: Place it directly over the bandage to save time
Leave the left arm lead unattached
Place it above the bandage and match the right
Place it on the right arm as well
questions.explain: The electrode is moved to an intact site nearby, and the electrode on the other limb is placed at a matching level. The change is noted on the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (special situations)
questions.q: Electrodes should generally be kept off which areas?
options: Broken skin, scars and bony areas
Fleshy parts of the lower legs
questions.explain: Broken skin, scar tissue and bony prominences give poor contact or discomfort, so nearby suitable sites are used and noted. Fleshy limb areas are preferred.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (machine settings)
questions.q: What should be entered into the EKG machine before recording?
questions.explain: Correct identifiers, age and sex let the tracing be filed properly and allow the machine's measurements to use the right reference values.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (machine settings)
questions.q: What is the purpose of the 60 Hz filter on an EKG machine?
options: To speed up the paper during the recording
questions.explain: The AC or 60 Hz filter reduces interference from power lines and electrical equipment. Filters should be used as directed because they can also slightly alter the tracing.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (machine settings)
questions.q: The machine prints a computer interpretation on the tracing. How should it be treated?
options: As a preliminary reading the provider confirms
As the final diagnosis to be placed in the chart
As information to share with the patient
As a reason to skip the provider review
questions.explain: Computer interpretations can be wrong, especially with artifact. A qualified provider over-reads and confirms the tracing; the technician does not interpret it for patients.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (machine settings)
questions.q: How many leads are displayed on a standard 12-lead tracing, and from how many electrodes?
questions.explain: The 10 electrodes produce 12 leads: three standard limb leads, three augmented leads and six chest leads. The right leg electrode is a reference.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (Holter monitor)
questions.q: How long is a standard Holter monitor commonly worn?
questions.explain: A Holter monitor continuously records the rhythm, typically for 24 to 48 hours. Monitors worn for weeks are usually event or extended patch monitors.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (Holter monitor)
questions.q: What should a patient record in the Holter diary?
options: Only the meals eaten each day
Nothing, since the device records all
Activities and symptoms with the times
questions.explain: The diary links symptoms such as palpitations or dizziness and activities to specific times, so the provider can compare them with the recorded rhythm.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (Holter monitor)
questions.q: Which instruction is commonly given to a patient wearing a Holter monitor?
options: Remove it at night so the patient can sleep better
Do not shower or bathe while wearing it
questions.explain: Most Holter recorders must stay dry, so patients are told not to shower, bathe or swim unless the device instructions allow it. The monitor stays on continuously.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (Holter monitor)
questions.q: Why is skin preparation especially important for a Holter monitor?
options: The patient will be lying still all day
Electrodes must stay attached for a long time
The monitor uses higher voltage than a 12-lead
Holter leads are placed on the limbs
questions.explain: The electrodes must stay securely attached for a day or more during normal activity. Good skin prep and securing lead wires reduce artifact and lost data.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (Holter monitor)
questions.q: When a patient returns the Holter monitor, what should be noted?
questions.explain: Noting the start and end times lets the recording be matched with the diary entries. The diary is collected with the device.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (event monitor)
questions.q: How does an event monitor differ from a standard Holter monitor?
options: It records only while the patient is asleep
It is used only in the hospital emergency room
It is worn longer and saves events when triggered
It records a single 12-lead tracing once
questions.explain: Event monitors are worn for weeks and save rhythm strips when the patient presses a button during symptoms, or automatically for some devices. A Holter records continuously for a shorter period.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: Which instruction is commonly given before an exercise stress test?
options: Eat a large meal right before the test for energy
Wear comfortable shoes and avoid a heavy meal
Wear dress shoes and a tight belt
Drink several cups of coffee first
questions.explain: Patients are usually told to wear comfortable clothes and walking shoes and to avoid heavy meals, and to follow the provider's instructions about caffeine and medications.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: Using the common formula, what is the estimated maximum heart rate of a 60-year-old patient?
questions.explain: The commonly taught estimate is 220 minus age, so 220 minus 60 equals 160 beats per minute. A target heart rate is often set at about 85 percent of this value.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: What is recorded before the patient begins exercising on the treadmill?
options: A resting EKG and blood pressure
questions.explain: Baseline resting EKG and blood pressure are recorded first so changes during exercise and recovery can be compared with them.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: In the commonly used Bruce protocol, what happens about every 3 minutes?
options: The patient stops walking to rest for a while
questions.explain: The Bruce protocol increases both speed and grade at roughly 3-minute stages to raise the workload. EKG, blood pressure and symptoms are monitored throughout every stage.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: A patient cannot walk on a treadmill but needs a stress test. What type of test may be ordered?
options: A test with the limb leads off
questions.explain: A pharmacologic stress test uses medication to stress the heart or increase blood flow when the patient cannot exercise adequately. It is supervised by a provider.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: Why are limb electrodes often placed on the torso for exercise stress testing?
options: To reduce motion artifact from the arms and legs
To make the test faster to set up for the technician
To avoid the need for skin prep
To lower the patient's heart rate
questions.explain: Torso placement of limb electrodes keeps them away from moving limbs and reduces motion artifact during exercise. The modified placement is noted.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (stress testing)
questions.q: After a treadmill stress test ends, how long is the patient monitored?
options: Only until the treadmill belt has come to a full stop
No monitoring is needed after the test
Only until the patient puts shoes on
Until heart rate, BP and EKG return toward baseline
questions.explain: Monitoring continues during recovery because abnormal rhythms or ST changes can appear after exercise. The patient is released when values approach baseline per protocol.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (telemetry)
questions.q: In a hospital unit, what is telemetry monitoring?
options: A single 12-lead EKG recorded with the patient at rest
Continuous remote monitoring of the rhythm
questions.explain: Telemetry transmits the heart rhythm continuously, often wirelessly, to a central station where it is watched. It usually uses 3 or 5 electrodes.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (telemetry)
questions.q: In the common US color code for a 5-lead monitoring system, which color goes on the right arm?
questions.explain: In the AHA color code used in the US, white is right arm, black is left arm, red is left leg, green is right leg and brown is the chest lead. "White on right" is a common memory aid.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (telemetry)
questions.q: A telemetry transmitter shows a low battery warning. What should be done?
options: Ignore it until the shift ends
Remove the electrodes from the patient
questions.explain: A dead battery stops monitoring, which could cause a missed rhythm. The battery is replaced promptly and the monitoring station is informed per policy.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (pacemakers)
questions.q: On a tracing from a patient with a pacemaker, what is the pacemaker spike?
options: A thin vertical line before the paced beat
A wide wandering baseline across the whole strip
questions.explain: A pacemaker spike is a narrow vertical line produced by the device's electrical stimulus, followed by the paced P wave or QRS. Some machine filters can make spikes harder to see.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead views)
questions.q: Which leads view the inferior wall of the heart?
questions.explain: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall. I, aVL, V5 and V6 view the lateral wall, V1 and V2 the septum and V3 and V4 the anterior wall.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (lead views)
questions.q: Which leads view the lateral wall of the left ventricle?
questions.explain: The lateral leads are I, aVL, V5 and V6. The inferior leads are II, III and aVF, and V1 and V2 are septal leads.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (electrode placement)
questions.q: Before removing electrodes, why does the technician check the printed tracing?
options: To interpret the rhythm for the patient before leaving
To decide on the patient's medications
To catch artifact or lead errors and repeat it
questions.explain: Reviewing the tracing for artifact, missing leads or reversal lets the technician correct problems and re-record before the patient leaves.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Acquisition (artifacts)
questions.q: A patient is cold and shivering in the exam room. What should the technician do before recording?
options: Offer a blanket and warm the room
questions.explain: Warming the patient reduces shivering, which causes somatic tremor artifact. Covering exposed areas also preserves privacy and helps the patient relax.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (EKG grid)
questions.q: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, how much time does one small box represent?
questions.explain: Each small 1 mm box equals 0.04 seconds at 25 mm per second. Five small boxes make one large box, which equals 0.20 seconds.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (EKG grid)
questions.q: At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, how much time does one large box represent?
questions.explain: One large box is five small boxes, so 5 times 0.04 equals 0.20 seconds. Five large boxes equal one second.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (EKG grid)
questions.q: At standard calibration, what voltage does one small box represent vertically?
questions.explain: At 10 mm per mV, each 1 mm small box represents 0.1 mV vertically. Ten small boxes, or two large boxes, equal 1 mV.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart rate)
questions.q: Using the 1500 method, there are 20 small boxes between two R waves in a regular rhythm. What is the heart rate?
questions.explain: The 1500 method divides 1500 by the number of small boxes between consecutive R waves: 1500 divided by 20 equals 75. The method works for regular rhythms.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart rate)
questions.q: Using the 300 method, there are 3 large boxes between R waves in a regular rhythm. What is the heart rate?
questions.explain: Dividing 300 by the number of large boxes between R waves gives the rate: 300 divided by 3 equals 100. The sequence 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50 is a quick memory aid.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart rate)
questions.q: A six-second strip shows 8 QRS complexes. What is the estimated heart rate?
questions.explain: The six-second method multiplies the number of QRS complexes in six seconds by 10, so 8 times 10 equals 80. This method works for irregular rhythms.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart rate)
questions.q: Which heart rate method is best suited to an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation?
options: Counting one R to R interval
questions.explain: Because R to R intervals vary in irregular rhythms, counting complexes in a six-second strip and multiplying by 10 gives a better estimate than measuring one interval.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (waveforms)
questions.q: What does the P wave represent?
questions.explain: The P wave reflects electrical activation of the atria. Ventricular depolarization is the QRS, ventricular repolarization is the T wave, and atrial repolarization is hidden in the QRS.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (waveforms)
questions.q: What does the QRS complex represent?
questions.explain: The QRS complex represents depolarization of the ventricles, which triggers ventricular contraction. The P wave is atrial depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (waveforms)
questions.q: What does the T wave represent?
questions.explain: The T wave reflects recovery, or repolarization, of the ventricles. It normally follows the ST segment after each QRS. The P wave and QRS represent depolarization instead.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (waveforms)
questions.q: Why is atrial repolarization not usually seen on the EKG?
options: It happens before the P wave in every cardiac cycle
It is too large to print
It appears only in lead aVR
It is hidden within the QRS complex
questions.explain: Atrial repolarization occurs at about the same time as ventricular depolarization, so the much larger QRS hides it. It is not a separate wave the technician measures.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (intervals)
questions.q: How is the PR interval measured?
options: From the end of the P wave to the end of the QRS
From the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS
From the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave
From one P wave to the next P wave
questions.explain: The PR interval runs from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex and reflects conduction from the atria through the AV node.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (intervals)
questions.q: What PR interval range is commonly taught as normal for adults?
questions.explain: A normal adult PR interval is commonly taught as 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, or 3 to 5 small boxes. A longer constant PR interval suggests a first-degree AV block.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (intervals)
questions.q: What QRS duration is commonly taught as normal for adults?
questions.explain: A normal QRS is commonly taught as less than 0.12 seconds, often about 0.06 to 0.10 seconds. A wider QRS suggests the impulse spread abnormally through the ventricles.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (intervals)
questions.q: A PR interval spans 4 small boxes. What is its duration?
questions.explain: Each small box is 0.04 seconds, so 4 boxes equal 0.16 seconds, within the commonly taught normal range of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (intervals)
questions.q: A QRS complex spans 2 small boxes. What is its duration?
questions.explain: Two small boxes times 0.04 seconds equals 0.08 seconds, which is a normal QRS duration because it is less than the commonly taught limit of 0.12 seconds.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: Which finding fits normal sinus rhythm in an adult?
options: Irregular rhythm without any visible P waves at all
Regular rate of 60 to 100 with a P before each QRS
Regular rate over 150 with wide QRS complexes
Sawtooth waves between the QRS complexes
questions.explain: Normal sinus rhythm is regular at 60 to 100 beats per minute, with an upright P wave before every QRS and normal intervals. The other choices describe atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia and atrial flutter.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A regular sinus rhythm has a rate of 48 beats per minute. What is it called?
questions.explain: Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm under 60 beats per minute. It can be normal in athletes but can also cause symptoms that need reporting.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A sinus rhythm has a rate of 120 beats per minute. What is it called?
questions.explain: Sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm over 100 beats per minute with normal P waves and narrow QRS complexes. Ventricular tachycardia has wide QRS complexes without related P waves.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A rhythm is irregularly irregular with no distinct P waves and a wavy baseline. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: Atrial fibrillation has chaotic atrial activity with fibrillatory waves instead of P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Atrial flutter shows regular sawtooth waves.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A tracing shows regular sawtooth-shaped waves between the QRS complexes. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: Atrial flutter produces regular flutter waves in a sawtooth pattern, often best seen in leads II, III and aVF. Atrial fibrillation has an irregular wavy baseline instead.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: An early, wide and bizarre QRS appears without a P wave before it, followed by a pause. What is it?
questions.explain: A PVC arises in the ventricles, so it comes early with a wide, unusual QRS, no preceding P wave and usually a compensatory pause. A premature atrial contraction has an early P wave and a narrow QRS.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: Every other beat on a strip is a PVC. What is this pattern called?
questions.explain: Bigeminy means every second beat is a PVC. In trigeminy every third beat is a PVC, a couplet is two PVCs in a row and three or more in a row is a run of ventricular tachycardia.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A rhythm shows wide, regular QRS complexes at about 180 beats per minute with no visible P waves. What does this most likely suggest?
questions.explain: Ventricular tachycardia is a fast, usually regular, wide-complex rhythm without related P waves. It can be life-threatening, so the technician checks the patient and notifies the provider immediately.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A tracing shows chaotic, irregular waves with no identifiable QRS complexes. What should the technician do first?
options: Print another copy of the tracing for the chart now
Check the patient for responsiveness and a pulse
Adjust the filter and record again later
Ask the patient to hold still and wait
questions.explain: This pattern suggests ventricular fibrillation, but artifact can look similar. The technician checks the patient immediately; an unresponsive pulseless patient needs a code call, CPR and defibrillation.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A monitor shows a flat line, but the patient is talking and alert. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A lead or electrode has come off
The patient is in ventricular fibrillation
The calibration is at double standard
questions.explain: An alert, talking patient cannot be in asystole, so a flat line points to a disconnected lead or electrode. The technician checks connections and confirms in more than one lead.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A patient is unresponsive and the tracing shows a flat line in more than one lead. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: A flat line confirmed in more than one lead in an unresponsive, pulseless patient indicates asystole, a cardiac arrest rhythm requiring an immediate code call and CPR.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart blocks)
questions.q: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, but the PR interval is constant at 0.28 seconds. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: A PR interval consistently longer than 0.20 seconds, with every P conducted, is first-degree AV block. In type II second-degree block some P waves are not followed by a QRS.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart blocks)
questions.q: The PR interval gets longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle repeats. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped QRS is second-degree type I, also called Wenckebach or Mobitz I. In type II the PR stays constant before a dropped beat.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart blocks)
questions.q: The PR interval stays the same, but some P waves are suddenly not followed by a QRS. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: Type II second-degree block, or Mobitz II, has constant PR intervals with sudden dropped QRS complexes. It can progress to complete heart block and is reported promptly.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (heart blocks)
questions.q: P waves and QRS complexes occur regularly but have no relationship to each other. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: In third-degree, or complete, heart block no atrial impulses reach the ventricles, so atria and ventricles beat independently. It often causes a slow rate and needs immediate reporting.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (critical findings)
questions.q: Which rhythm requires immediate notification and emergency response?
questions.explain: Ventricular fibrillation produces no effective cardiac output and is a cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate CPR and defibrillation. The other choices are usually benign.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (critical findings)
questions.q: On a patient's 12-lead, the technician notices ST segments clearly elevated in leads II, III and aVF. What should be done?
options: Notify the provider or nurse immediately
File the tracing with routine work
Tell the patient a heart attack is happening
questions.explain: ST elevation in related leads can indicate an acute heart attack, so the tracing is brought to the provider or nurse immediately. Diagnosis and explanation to the patient are the provider's role.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: In a young adult, the heart rate speeds up with inhalation and slows with exhalation. What is this rhythm called?
questions.explain: Sinus arrhythmia is a sinus rhythm whose rate varies with breathing, common and usually normal in young people. Each beat still has a normal P wave before the QRS.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: A very fast, regular rhythm at about 180 beats per minute has narrow QRS complexes. What does this most likely suggest?
questions.explain: A narrow QRS shows the impulse travels the normal ventricular pathway, so a very fast regular narrow-complex rhythm suggests supraventricular tachycardia. Ventricular tachycardia has wide complexes.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: Which finding helps identify a rhythm as sinus in origin?
options: A QRS wider than 0.12 seconds in most of the leads
An upright P wave in lead II before each QRS
No P waves visible in any lead
questions.explain: Sinus rhythms start in the SA node, producing an upright P wave in lead II before every QRS. Absent P waves and sawtooth waves point to other atrial rhythms.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (waveforms)
questions.q: What is the isoelectric line on an EKG?
options: The tallest point of the R wave in each QRS complex
The line formed by the calibration pulse
The line that marks one second
The flat baseline with no net electrical activity
questions.explain: The isoelectric line is the flat baseline between waveforms, where no net electrical activity is recorded. Elevation or depression of segments is judged against it.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: Two PVCs occur back to back on a strip. What is this called?
questions.explain: Two consecutive PVCs form a couplet. Bigeminy and trigeminy describe PVCs alternating with normal beats in patterns, and three or more PVCs in a row are a run of ventricular tachycardia.

questions.ref: NHA CET test plan (2017), EKG Analysis and Interpretation (rhythm recognition)
questions.q: How can the technician check whether a rhythm is regular?
options: Compare R to R intervals across the strip
Count only the P waves that appear in lead aVR
Measure the height of a single T wave
Look only at the calibration mark
questions.explain: Measuring successive R to R intervals with calipers or marked paper shows whether they are equal. Regularity helps identify the rhythm and choose a rate method.
